title: Spacewar! and its real star map
hook: An early video game from MIT used a real star chart for its background.
peek: Spacewar, written at MIT in 1962, pitted two spaceships against each other on a round screen. Behind them scrolled the real night sky, drawn from an astronomers' almanac, in a part of the program jokingly named the Expensive Planetarium.
lede: In 1962, a group of young programmers at MIT wrote Spacewar for the university's new PDP-1 computer. Two players each steered a small spaceship around a round screen. The game could have used random dots for stars, but the programmer Peter Samson put in the real sky instead, carefully copied from a star chart, so players flew across actual constellations.

bullets.text: Samson's star display was called the Expensive Planetarium, a joke on the cost of the PDP-1 and on other MIT programs with names like Expensive Typewriter. The stars drifted slowly across the screen as the night sky does.
The star positions came from an astronomers' almanac, and the display showed the brighter stars of a band of sky. People who knew the night sky could pick out real constellations.

Steve Russell wrote most of the game, from an idea he worked out with Martin Graetz and Wayne Wiitanen. Others added parts, including a star at the centre whose gravity pulled the ships in, and a hyperspace escape button.

The game spread to other PDP-1 computers, and its maker, Digital Equipment Corporation, used it to show off and test new machines. Russell never earned money from it, but Spacewar inspired the first arcade games.
